summary: Describes Layered Coding Transport, a building block that gives transport-level support for reliable content delivery and stream delivery protocols. It is designed for IP multicast but also supports unicast, and works with multiple-rate congestion control and coding techniques. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 5651.

eli5.summary: This is one of the Lego pieces for sending the same file to many receivers at once. It handles the basic labels on each packet. It was replaced by RFC 5651.

subtitle: A transport-level building block for scalable, reliable delivery of files and streams over IP multicast.

tldr.problem: Sending one file or stream to many receivers at once over IP multicast needs a standard way to organize packets, handle different data rates, and identify which session and object each packet belongs to.
tldr.mechanism: LCT provides a common header format for multicast packets with fields for session identification, object identification, congestion control information, and optional timing fields. It is combined with other building blocks like coding schemes and congestion control protocols to form complete protocols.
tldr.outcome: LCT became an experimental building block for scalable multicast applications but was later replaced by RFC 5651 as part of a more complete NORM (Nack-Oriented Reliable Multicast) framework.

facts.label: Header type
facts.value: Variable length, beginning with version and flags

facts.label: Optional fields
facts.value: Transport Object ID, Sender Current Time, Expected Residual Time

today: RFC 3451 is marked Experimental and was replaced by RFC 5651, which integrated LCT into the broader NORM (Nack-Oriented Reliable Multicast) framework and refined the specification based on operational experience.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Layered Coding Transport (LCT) is a building block that provides transport-level support for reliable content delivery and stream delivery protocols. LCT is designed specifically for IP multicast (sending one stream to many receivers at once), but also works with unicast (one-to-one). The protocol is designed for massively scalable delivery: it avoids mechanisms like receiver feedback that would not scale to many thousands of receivers.

LCT is not a complete protocol by itself. It is a building block that must be combined with other components: a congestion control protocol (to adapt transmission rate to network conditions), optionally a reliability mechanism (like forward error correction), and session control. LCT handles the common transport-level concerns that all multicast delivery applications need.
sections.eli5: LCT is a template for labeling multicast packets. Different applications combine it with other pieces (like error-fixing codes and speed control) to make complete protocols.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
LCT organizes delivery into sessions and objects. A session is a logical grouping of related transmissions from one sender. Within a session, the sender may transmit one or more objects, which could be files to download or streams to watch. For example, a weather service might have one session delivering a new weather map (an object) each hour.

LCT sessions can use layering for congestion control and quality variation. A sender transmits a session over multiple LCT channels, each at a different rate. Receivers can join any subset of these channels. A receiver joining more channels gets higher quality or faster delivery. For example, a video session might have three layers: basic quality on channel 1, better quality by adding channel 2, and high definition by adding channel 3. Receivers adapt their layer subscriptions based on available bandwidth.

The main advantage of layering is scalability: each receiver independently joins and leaves channels based on its network conditions, without needing to send feedback to the sender or coordinate with other receivers.
sections.eli5: LCT divides a delivery session into multiple quality levels (layers). Slow receivers take just the basic layer, fast receivers take more layers for better quality. Each receiver picks which layers it wants without asking permission.

sections.title: The LCT Header
sections.content:
Every LCT packet includes a variable-length LCT header that identifies the packet and carries session-level information. The header always includes a version field and flags that indicate which optional fields are present.

The Transmission Session Identifier (TSI) is a required field that identifies which session the packet belongs to. The TSI is scoped by the sender's IP address, so the pair (sender IP, TSI) uniquely identifies a session. For UDP-based protocols, the UDP source port can serve as the TSI.

The Transport Object Identifier (TOI) is an optional field that identifies which object (file, stream segment, etc.) the packet carries data for. This allows a receiver to track multiple concurrent objects within a session.

The Congestion Control Information (CCI) field carries data needed for the congestion control algorithm to work. The exact meaning of the CCI field is determined by the congestion control protocol being used with LCT.

Optional fields include Sender Current Time (SCT), which tells when the sender created the packet, and Expected Residual Time (ERT), which tells how much longer the session will continue. These help receivers understand session timing and decide whether to keep waiting for more packets.
sections.eli5: The LCT header is the label on each packet. It says which session it belongs to, which file/stream it is for, and how fast the sender is sending.

sections.title: Applications and Reliability
sections.content:
LCT is most useful for delivering large objects or long streams: files measured in megabytes to gigabytes, or streams lasting tens of seconds or more. It is efficient for both push services (where the sender continuously transmits and receivers join when they want) and on-demand services (where a sender transmits for a fixed period until all interested receivers have received the content).

Because LCT runs over unreliable best-effort delivery (IP multicast), a complete protocol needs a reliability mechanism. LCT does not define this itself but is designed to work with forward error correction (FEC) coding. With FEC, a receiver needs to collect only a threshold number of packets to reconstruct the original data, regardless of which packets are lost. This avoids the scalability problem of retransmission requests from many receivers.

For example, to deliver a 50 MB file on a low-speed channel, a sender might transmit 50,000 packets of 1 KB each. The receiver collects whichever packets arrive and reconstructs the file once enough have been received. By adding more LCT channels with additional redundant packets, faster receivers can complete the download sooner.
sections.eli5: LCT works well for big files or long streams. To handle lost packets, it can be paired with error-correction codes that let receivers reconstruct data from any subset of packets received.

viz.caption: Layered delivery: receivers join multiple channels for higher quality

layers.label: LCT Channel 1 (base)
layers.detail: Sent to all receivers at minimum rate

layers.label: LCT Channel 2 (enhancement)
layers.detail: Optional; receivers join if bandwidth available

layers.label: LCT Channel 3 (high quality)
layers.detail: Highlight channel; fast receivers join for best quality

layers.label: LCT Channel 4+ (optional layers)
layers.detail: Additional refinement layers if scalable congestion control supports them

fields.name: Version (V), Congestion fields (C), flags (r,S,O,H,T,R,A,B)
fields.desc: Version and feature flags indicating which optional fields are present.

fields.name: Header Length (HDR_LEN)
fields.desc: Length of the LCT header in 32-bit words.

fields.name: Codepoint (CP)
fields.desc: Identifies the codec or reliability mechanism used.

fields.name: Congestion Control Info (CCI)
fields.desc: Variable length; carries information for the congestion control protocol.

fields.name: Transport Session ID (TSI)
fields.desc: Identifies the session; scoped by sender IP address.

fields.name: Transport Object ID (TOI)
fields.desc: Optional; identifies which object the packet carries data for.

fields.name: Sender Current Time (SCT)
fields.desc: Optional; time the packet was sent (useful for real-time streams).

fields.name: Expected Residual Time (ERT)
fields.desc: Optional; how much longer the session will continue.
